content: This report is being published as a courtesy to both the National Association of State Public Health Veterinarians, Inc., and the MMWR readership. Its publication does not imply endorsement by the CDC. The purpose of this compendium is to provide detailed information about rabies to veterinarians, public health officials, and other professionals involved in rabies prevention and control. These recommendations form the foundation for animal rabies-control programs across the United States and aim to standardize procedures among different jurisdictions, thereby contributing to a cohesive and effective national rabies-control program. This document is reviewed annually and updated as necessary. Recommendations for vaccination procedures are outlined in Part I. Part II lists all animal rabies vaccines licensed by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) and available in the United States. Part III explains the principles of rabies control. Part I: Recommendations for Parenteral Vaccination Procedures A. Vaccine Administration All animal rabies vaccines should only be administered by, or under the direct supervision of, a licensed veterinarian. B. Vaccine Selection Part II of this document lists all USDA-licensed rabies vaccines available in the United States at the time of publication. Any new vaccine approvals or changes to label specifications after publication should also be considered part of this list. Vaccines used in state and local rabies-control programs should provide a 3-year duration of immunity, as this is the most effective way to increase the proportion of immunized dogs and cats in a population. C. Route of Inoculation All rabies vaccines must be administered strictly according to the instructions provided on the product label or package insert. Any adverse reactions or vaccine failures should be reported to the USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, Center for Veterinary Biologics, either by phone at (800) 752-6255 or via email at CVB@usda.gov. D. Wildlife and Hybrid Animal Vaccination The effectiveness of parenteral rabies vaccination in wildlife and hybrid animals (offspring of wild animals crossbred with domestic dogs or cats) has not been established, and no vaccines are currently licensed for use in these animals. E. F. Identification of Vaccinated Animals Veterinarians and agencies may use a standardized tag system to verify an animal’s rabies vaccination status. Rabies Tags: Canvassing: Citations: Legal citations may be issued to pet owners for failing to vaccinate or license their animals. This authority should be an integral part of any animal-control program. Animal Control: A. Dogs, Cats, and Ferrets Unvaccinated animals: Dogs, cats, and ferrets that are unvaccinated and exposed to a rabid animal should be euthanized immediately. If the owner refuses, the animal must be placed in strict isolation for six months and vaccinated one month before release. Animals with expired vaccinations: These cases should be evaluated individually. Currently vaccinated animals: These animals should be revaccinated immediately, kept under the owner’s control, and observed for 45 days. B. Livestock Vaccinated livestock: Livestock exposed to rabies and currently vaccinated with a USDA-approved vaccine should be revaccinated immediately and observed for 45 days. Unvaccinated livestock: These animals should be slaughtered immediately. If the owner refuses, the animal must be closely observed for six months. If slaughtered within seven days of being bitten, the animal’s tissues may be consumed safely, provided the exposed area is discarded. Tissues or milk from a rabid animal should not be consumed. Pasteurization inactivates the rabies virus, so pasteurized milk or cooked meat does not pose a risk. Rabies transmission within a herd is rare, so restricting the rest of the herd may not be necessary. C. Other Animals Other mammals bitten by a rabid animal should be euthanized immediately. Animals housed in USDA-licensed research facilities or accredited zoological parks should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. Management of Animals That Bite Humans A. Dogs, Cats, and Ferrets A healthy dog, cat, or ferret that bites a person should be confined and observed daily for 10 days. Rabies vaccination should not be administered during this observation period. If the animal shows signs of illness, it should be evaluated by a veterinarian immediately. Any illness suggestive of rabies should be reported to the local health department. If rabies is suspected, the animal should be euthanized, and its head sent to a qualified laboratory for rabies testing. Stray or unwanted animals that bite a person may be euthanized immediately, and their heads submitted for rabies examination. B. Other Animals Other biting animals that may have exposed a person to rabies should be reported to the local health department. Prior vaccination does not necessarily eliminate the need for euthanasia and testing, as the period of virus shedding is unknown for many species. Management depends on the species, the circumstances of the bite, the local rabies epidemiology, and the animal’s health and history. Control Methods Among Wildlife The public should be advised not to handle wildlife. Wild mammals and hybrids that bite or expose humans, pets, or livestock should be euthanized and tested for rabies. A. Terrestrial Mammals Oral rabies vaccines licensed for wildlife may be used in specific situations with approval from the state agency responsible for rabies control. Continuous government-funded programs for trapping or poisoning wildlife are not cost-effective for statewide rabies control but may be appropriate in high-contact areas such as parks or suburban regions. State agriculture, public health, and wildlife agencies should collaborate on planning and evaluating vaccination or population-reduction programs. B. Bats Rabid bats have been reported in every state except Hawaii and have caused rabies in at least 33 humans in the United States. Bats should be excluded from homes and nearby structures to prevent human contact. Once excluded, these structures should be sealed to prevent reentry. Programs aimed at reducing bat populations are neither feasible nor desirable for rabies control.
